entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• Timothy was one of Paul's most trusted co-workers and messengers. Paul lists Timothy as a co-sender for five other letters: 

• 2 Corinthians

• Colossians

• 1 Thessalonians

• 2 Thessalonians

• Philemon

• servants of Christ Jesus: Paul and Timothy belonged entirely to Christ and were fully devoted to his service (see Philippians 2:20–21). 

• God's holy people are made holy in God's sight by Christ's redeeming work (see Ephesians 1:4, Ephesians 1:7; Ephesians 5:25–27; Colossians 1:22). They are being made holy by the transforming work of the Holy Spirit in their lives (compare Philippians 4:21). 

• Philippi was a Roman colony in the province of Macedonia. The church in Philippi was the first Christian community in Greece (see Acts 16:11–40). 

• In the early church, church leaders provided spiritual guidance, while deacons attended to practical matters (see 1 Timothy 3:1–13). There were no pastors or priests who did this work as their regular paid job, as some do today (compare 1 Corinthians 14:26–31).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Paul begins his letter by listing the senders and recipients. He then offers a blessing of grace and peace.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Grace is the kindness and blessing God gives, even though people do not deserve it. Peace means deep well-being and calmness that come from the good news about Jesus and are produced by the Holy Spirit (see Galatians 5:22). Both grace and peace are gifts from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ (see Romans 5:1–2).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Paul thanks God for the recipients and prays for them. This is Paul's usual practice when writing letters.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Paul felt joy because the Philippians partnered with him to spread the good news about Jesus. Paul was confident that God would continue his good work in them.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Their partnership also included giving money to help Paul in his work (refer to Philippians 4:10–20).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: He who began a good work in you: It is God who starts his saving work in people (see Romans 9:16; Ephesians 1:3–8, Ephesians 1:11; Ephesians 2:4–10). Because God is the one who began it, we can trust that God will continue changing believers to become more like his Son (see Romans 8:29; Ephesians 4:13, Ephesians 4:15).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: you are all partners in grace with me: Perhaps their lives were blessed because of Paul’s suffering and witness. Perhaps they had suffered together with him (see Philippians 1:29).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• Love is the result of Christ’s Spirit within believers (Romans 5:5; Galatians 5:22). Love is part of the fruit of the Spirit. The fruit of the Spirit is the evidence that Christ is working in believers

• abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight: Growing in understanding helps believers know what truly matters (see Romans 12:2). It helps them live pure and blameless lives until Christ returns (compare 1 Thessalonians 3:12–13; 1 Thessalonians 5:23).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• People cannot create righteous character on their own; it only comes through the Spirit of Christ working in their hearts. 

• The ultimate purpose for God's people is to give glory and praise to God (see Ephesians 1:6, Ephesians 1:12, Ephesians 1:14).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• brothers: Paul uses the Greek word adelphoi, which was a common way to speak to a group of fellow believers (both men and women) as part of God’s family.

• my circumstances: This refers to Paul's imprisonment.

• have actually served to advance the gospel: See Acts 28:17–31 for an example of this.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Paul was happy that his time in prison helped spread the good news about Jesus.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• the whole palace guard: These were soldiers who worked in the official residence of the emperor or a Roman governor (see Philippians 4:22). 

• Paul was in prison for preaching the good news of Christ (compare Acts 21:26–28:31).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Paul’s courage while in prison helped most of the brothers (fellow believers; see study note on 1:12) trust in the Lord. They became more courageous and spoke God’s message without fear.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry: These people were likely other believers who did not like Paul and criticized him (see 2 Corinthians 10:2 Corinthians 10–13; Galatians 4:12–20; Galatians 5:7–12). Even so, the message about Christ was being preached, so Paul rejoiced.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: will turn out for my deliverance: Paul expected to be released from prison soon (see Philippians 1:25–26; Philippians 2:24). This is different from what Paul wrote later in 2 Timothy 4:6, when he was in prison again and expected to die.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: to die is gain: For believers, death is not something to fear. It means going to be with Christ (see Philippians 1:23; compare John 5:24; John 11:25–26; Romans 8:38–39).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: I desire to depart and be with Christ: Death leads believers immediately into the Lord’s presence (see Philippians 3:20–21; 1 Corinthians 15:20–23, 1 Corinthians 15:51–52; 2 Corinthians 5:1–8; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–17).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• The well-being of the church is more important to Paul than his own desire to be with Christ. 

• for your progress and joy in the faith: Christians should find joy even during tough times (see Philippians 4:4; John 15:11, John 15:20; John 16:20–24; 1 Thessalonians 5:16).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: As foreigners in this world, the Philippian believers should live like citizens of heaven (compare Philippians 3:20; 1 Peter 2:9–11).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Paul encourages the Christians in Philippi to live in a way that honors the gospel (see Ephesians 4:1; Colossians 1:10; 1 Thessalonians 2:12). He especially encourages them to stay strong and faithful, even when they face persecution.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: This is a clear sign of their destruction but of your salvation: The Philippians’ courage is a sign that their opponents will be destroyed and that the Philippians themselves will be saved. The same Greek phrase could also mean a sign to them that you are going to be destroyed, but a sign to you that you are going to be saved. According to that interpretation, those who persecute the believers would still not recognize the truth (compare 2 Corinthians 2:15–16).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: For it has been granted to you … to suffer for Him: What the world sees as shameful, Christians see as an honor because it is for Christ. It honors him.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• you are encountering the same struggle: Both Paul and the Philippians faced strong opposition. Paul was in prison, and the Philippians were being persecuted. 

• the same struggle you saw I had: See Acts 16:11–40; compare 1 Thessalonians 2:2.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: If any ...? These are rhetorical questions that expect a “yes” answer. Paul is saying that if people have truly experienced Christ, they should live together with love, unity, and care for one another.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: During their persecution, Paul urges the Philippians to be united and live a humble life like Christ.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Do nothing out of selfish ambition: Thinking only about yourself is the opposite of truly caring for others (compare Philippians 2:20–21; 1 Corinthians 10:24; Galatians 5:26).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: existing in the form of God: Jesus has the same nature as God and has existed with him from the beginning (see John 1:1–3; John 17:5; Colossians 1:15).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
This early Christian hymn is about:

• Christ’s divine nature and existence before the world began, 

• Christ's coming to earth as a human and dying, and

• Christ's exaltation and role as Lord over all.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• he emptied himself: He gave up his divine privileges and chose to live as a human. The rest of verses Philippians 2:7–8 explains this ultimate act of godly self-giving love (compare 2 Corinthians 8:9). 

• taking the form of a servant: Paul might have been thinking of Isaiah 52:13–53:12. 

• being made in human likeness: Jesus became truly human while still being God (see John 1:14; 1 Timothy 3:16).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• He humbled Himself and became obedient to death: Jesus obeyed God’s will by dying for the sins of humanity (see Isaiah 53:7; Matthew 26:39; John 3:16; John 10:17–18; Romans 5:8, Romans 5:19; Romans 8:3; Hebrews 5:8; 1 John 4:9–10, 1 John 4:14). 

• even death on a cross: Death on a cross was a death specifically for criminals. In the Roman Empire, crucifixion was a cruel and humiliating punishment for criminals.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• Therefore: Because of Christ's humble obedience, God raised him to the place of highest honor (see Acts 1:9–10; compare Acts 2:32–33; Acts 7:55–56). 

• gave Him the name above all names: Jesus has supreme authority and power (Philippians 2:10–11; compare Matthew 28:18; John 17:5; Acts 2:33–36; Hebrews 2:9; Hebrews 12:2).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• in heaven and on earth and under the earth: All of creation, including spiritual powers, angels, humans on earth, and those who have died, will one day acknowledge Jesus Christ's authority as Lord (see Ephesians 1:9–10, Ephesians 1:21; Colossians 1:20–25; 1 Peter 3:22). 

• every tongue confess (compare Isaiah 45:23; Romans 14:11): This does not mean everyone will be saved. Not everyone will confess Jesus as Lord willingly out of love and devotion. 

• Jesus Christ is Lord: God's personal name in the Old Testament, Yahweh, was considered too holy to say aloud. So Jewish people would say Adonai (which means “Lord”) instead. When the Old Testament was translated into Greek, Yahweh was represented by the Greek word kurios (“Lord”). This same title is often used for Jesus in the New Testament.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: as you have always obeyed (see John 3:36; Romans 1:5): Believers must consider God's judgment like everyone else (compare 1 Corinthians 3:10–13). Therefore, they should live obediently before God, with deep respect and fear.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Paul encourages believers to stay strong in their faith and live lives of obedience and purity, following Christ's example.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: For it is God who works in you: God gives believers the strength and energy to live their lives (see John 15:5; 1 Corinthians 12:6; 1 Corinthians 15:10; 2 Corinthians 3:5; 1 Thessalonians 2:13). The desire and ability to do what pleases God come from God.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Complaining and arguing come from thinking only about yourself (see 1 Corinthians 10:10; 1 Peter 4:9; Jude 1:16). God calls believers to love others in a way that puts their needs first (Philippians 2:4).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• you shine as lights in the world: Believers should attract others to God through their actions (see Matthew 5:13–16). 

• in a crooked and perverse generation: See Deuteronomy 32:5; Romans 1:18–32; Romans 3:10–23.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• hold forth the word of life: Believers must keep trusting in the good news about Jesus, which gives life. God is faithful, but believers must also remain faithful (Philippians 1:6; Philippians 2:12–13). 

• that I did not run or labor in vain: Paul often compares the Christian life to running a race or training for a competition (see Philippians 3:12–14; 1 Corinthians 9:24, 1 Corinthians 9:26; Galatians 2:2; Galatians 5:7; 2 Timothy 4:7).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• even if I am being poured out like a drink offering … I am glad and rejoice: In both Jewish and pagan traditions, people would pour out wine on a sacrifice or at the altar to honor their god. Paul uses this image to say that his whole life is like an offering to God (compare Romans 12:1; Romans 15:16). 

• Faithful service brings joy because nothing done for God is wasted (see 1 Corinthians 15:58).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Paul praises Timothy, whome he hopes to send to the Philippians in the near future. Timothy traveled with Paul on his first trip to Philippi (see Acts 16:1–3, Acts 16:12; Acts 17:15; Acts 18:5; compare Acts 19:22). Timothy was known for dedicating his life to Jesus Christ and caring for others.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: what happens with me: This might refer to the result of Paul's trial.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Paul was confident that he would soon be released from prison by the Roman authorities and visit the Philippians (see Philippians 1:19, Philippians 1:25–26).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• Paul praises Epaphroditus, a messenger from the church at Philippi (see also Philippians 4:18). Paul is now sending Epaphroditus back to Philippi, perhaps with this letter. 

• Paul describes Epaphroditus as his fellow soldier. This suggests the challenges, opposition, and dangers faced in Christ's work.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Paul believed God showed mercy by helping Epaphroditus recover from a serious illness. This mercy also helped Paul, who was already suffering in prison.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Epaphroditus deserved their honor because he risked his life for Christ on their behalf (for the importance of showing honor, compare Romans 10:12; Romans 13:7; Ephesians 5:33; Ephesians 6:2; 1 Timothy 5:17; 1 Timothy 6:1; 1 Peter 2:17; 1 Peter 3:7).

entries.title: Philippians
Philippians
entries.content: those dogs, those workers of evil: Here, Paul reverses the traditional Jewish practice of calling non-Jewish people dogs (see Mark 7:27–28). Paul directs his strongest insults at Jews who taught that non-Jewish people must be circumcised to be saved (see 2 Corinthians 11:13–15; Galatians 1:6–9; Galatians 5:1–6, Galatians 5:12).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Paul warns believers not to be influenced by Jewish Christians who say circumcision is necessary for salvation. Paul then talks about his own conversion from Judaism to following Christ.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Circumcision was a sign that someone belonged to God’s people (see Gen 17:10–14). But the Bible teaches that those who trust in Christ are the ones who are truly circumcised in their hearts (see Romans 2:28–29; compare Jeremiah 4:4; Ephesians 2:11; Colossians 2:11–13). Being circumcised in heart means we are changed on the inside. Our hearts are made new by God so they can love and obey him.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: in the flesh: Paul uses flesh to mean relying on yourself and human effort. This is different than relying on Christ and the power given by the Spirit.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• circumcised on the eighth day: This followed Jewish law, which required boys to be circumcised on the eighth day (See Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3; Luke 1:59; Luke 2:21).

• Paul belonged to the Pharisees, a Jewish group known for strictly following the law (see Acts 23:6; Acts 26:5).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: If anyone had reason to trust in their religious status as a Jew, Paul did. He strictly followed Jewish law and was very passionate about the Jewish religion.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• as to zeal, persecuting the church (see Acts 8:1–3; Acts 9:1–2, Acts 9:21; Galatians 1:13): Paul's actions showed his strong support for Judaism, which saw the good news about Jesus as a threat. 

• Paul’s righteousness, as judged by human standards, also showed his dedication to the law (see also Galatians 1:14; for Paul’s later Christian view, compare Romans 3:23; Romans 7:14–25).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: As a Christian, Paul now considered these things (Philippians 3:5–6) worthless because of what Christ has done. A believer’s relationship with God is defined by knowing Christ and nothing else (compare Philippians 3:10; John 17:3). The only important thing is to gain Christ, thus receiving the gift of eternal salvation (see John 3:16; 1 John 5:11–13). In comparison, all other things are meaningless garbage (or rubbish).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• Paul explains the difference between his view of salvation and that of his opponents (Philippians 3:2). 

• Believers unite with Christ by trusting him for salvation and sharing in his life (see John 15:1–5). 

• We become righteous not by following the law of Moses, but through faith in Christ. This is God's way of making us right with him: Salvation is a free gift, not something we can earn (see Romans 1:17; Romans 3:21–26; Romans 4:5–8; Galatians 2:16; Ephesians 2:8–9).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• to know Christ: By knowing Jesus Christ, a person knows and is accepted by God (compare Philippians 3:7–8; John 1:12–13; John 17:3). 

• Believers experience the mighty power that raised Christ from the dead, both now and in eternity (see Romans 6:4–14; Romans 8:10–11; Colossians 3:1–4). 

• the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to Him in His death: United with Christ, a believer has the privilege of experiencing his life and death (see Philippians 1:29; 2 Corinthians 4:10–12; Colossians 1:24; 1 Peter 4:13–16).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Experiencing resurrection from the dead means being saved from judgment and receiving eternal life (see Revelation 20:4–6). Paul understood God's holiness and the seriousness of the final judgment (Revelation 20:11–15). He knew he must continue to pursue Christ and salvation (compare Galatians 5:5).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Using himself as an example, Paul encourages the Philippians to pursue Christ and the hope of heaven with determination and strength.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• I press on toward the goal: Paul compares the Christian life to a race. Just as a runner keeps going to reach the finish line, Paul keeps following Christ with hope of the final reward (see study note on 2:16). 

• Paul was ready to give up everything for the ultimate goal, the heavenly prize of eternal life.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Spiritually mature people (see 1 Corinthians 2:6; 1 Corinthians 3:1) agree with Paul that eternal things matter most in life (Philippians 3:12–14; compare 2 Corinthians 4:16–18).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: we must live up to what we have already attained: Believers should not go backward in their faith. Their way of life should match what they have already learned about Christ.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Join one another in following my example: Paul seriously pursued Christ and the life God called him to (Philippians 3:7–14; Philippians 4:9; 1 Corinthians 4:6, 1 Corinthians 4:16–17; 1 Corinthians 11:1; 2 Thessalonians 3:7–9). This is very different from the enemies of Christ who are described next (Philippians 3:18–19).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ: The identity of the enemies is not certain. They may have been: 

• Jews or Jewish Christians who were proud of their circumcision (as in Philippians 3:2) and who emphasized Judaism in a way that did not agree with the message of the cross of Christ;

• false believers living in a worldly and immoral way (see Philippians 3:19); or

• people who claimed to believe but rejected Paul’s teaching that the good news centers on Christ’s death on the cross (see 1 Corinthians 1:23; compare Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• their god is their belly: This phrase may refer to their greed, sexcual desires, or self-interest (compare Romans 16:18). 

• their glory is in their shame: This most likely refers to immoral behavior, not to pride in circumcision.

• Eternal destruction is God's ultimate judgment for those who reject Christ and live selfish, sinful lives (see 2 Thessalonians 1:8–9; compare Philippians 1:28; Matthew 7:13; Romans 9:22; 1 Corinthians 1:18; 2 Thessalonians 2:10; 1 Timothy 6:9; 2 Peter 2:3, 2 Peter 2:13; Jude 1:10; Revelation 11:18). 

• their minds are set on earthly things: They cannot see beyond this life (compare John 12:25; 1 John 2:15–17).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: In contrast, believers know that their true home is in heaven with the Lord Jesus Christ (see Ephesians 2:19). So they focus their thoughts on heavenly things (see Colossians 3:1–2; compare 1 Corinthians 15:19; 1 Peter 2:11). They also focus their thoughts on Christ’s return (see 1 Corinthians 1:7; Titus 2:13).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body: When Jesus returns, he will transform believers' physical bodies. Instead of weak, aging bodies that die, they will have perfect, eternal bodies (see 1 Corinthians 15:42–54; compare Romans 8:23). 

• enables Him to subject all things to Himself: This means that Jesus will have complete authority over all things. Everything in creation will be subject to his rule (see 1 Corinthians 15:24–27).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• stand firm in the Lord: This means to remain faithful and committed to Jesus Christ (compare Philippians 1:27). 

• Their ongoing faithfulness to Christ brought Paul great joy and was the reward for his hard work (see 1 Thessalonians 2:19–20).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: agree with each other in the Lord: The Lord's people should live in peace with one another (see Philippians 2:2; 1 Corinthians 1:10; Ephesians 4:1–3, Ephesians 4:31–32; Colossians 3:12–15). We do not know what the disagreement between Euodia and Syntyche was about.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Before ending the letter, Paul discusses a small conflict in the church and writes a few words of encouragement.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• my true yokefellow (or loyal Syzygus): The Greek word suzuge is either a personal name or a description. We do not know exactly who this person was. 

• Nothing more is known about Clement. 

• whose names are in the Book of Life: Those whose names are written in the Book of Life are true believers. God will give them eternal life (see Luke 10:20; Revelation 3:5; Revelation 13:8; Revelation 17:8; Revelation 20:12, Revelation 20:15; Revelation 21:27; compare Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• In Paul’s letters, joy and rejoicing are a response to hearing the good news about Jesus (see Ephesians 5:19–20). Joy does not depend on circumstances. Instead, believers can have joy even when life is difficult.

• Rejoice! This is a command Paul often gives to Christians (see Philippians 2:18; Philippians 3:1; Romans 12:12, Romans 12:15; 1 Thessalonians 5:16).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Rejoice … by prayer and petition … with thanksgiving: Compare with 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18. Both passages were written to churches facing persecution (see also Romans 12:12).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Believers should treat others with kindness and thoughtfulness, when those people are treating them badly or causing them to suffer for their faith. Believers do not need to seek revenge or try to get back at people who hurt them. Instead, they can trust that God will handle justice in his own time and way. Believers can act this way because they believe Jesus will return soon (see James 5:8–9).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Believers do not need to worry, because their Father in heaven loves them and takes care of their needs. He invites them to pray about everything (see Matthew 6:25–34; Matthew 7:9–11; Romans 12:12; Ephesians 6:18; 1 Thessalonians 5:17; 1 Peter 5:7).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Those who trust God (see Philippians 4:6) will experience God's peace (see also Isaiah 26:3; John 14:27; Colossians 3:15).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Paul urges the Philippians to focus on God's good gifts. Then, even when they suffer and are treated badly by others, they can live in a way that honors God and have peace in their hearts and mind (Philippians 4:7, Philippians 4:9).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Whatever you have learned or received or heard from me: This refers to everything Paul had taught them by word and example about the kind of life God wants us to live (see Philippians 3:17; 1 Corinthians 4:6, 1 Corinthians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 3:7–9).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: It is not clear why they were not able to help him earlier.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: At the end of the letter, Paul thanks the Philippians for the gift they sent him through Epaphroditus.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: As a servant of Christ, Paul has learned to be content with every situation, whether he had plenty or little. His life was filled with the joy that comes from doing the will of God whatever the cost.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: through Christ: With Christ's help, Paul had the strength to do everything. In all situations, Paul relied on the strength of Christ, who lived in him and worked through him. This was especially true during times of suffering (see 2 Corinthians 1:8–10; 2 Corinthians 4:7–12; 2 Corinthians 12:8–10; Galatians 2:20; Colossians 1:27).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: The Philippians showed kindness and generosity, which was especially meaningful because Paul was suffering in prison.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving: Paul chose not to accept money from the Corinthians, because he was concerned it might harm how they understood the good news about Jesus (1 Corinthians 9:11–18; 2 Corinthians 11:7–12). But he had no such concern with the Philippians. 

• in the early days of the gospel: This refers to when Paul first preached the good news in Philippi (See Acts 16:11–40).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: After Paul left Philippi (see Philippians 4:15), he traveled to Thessalonica (see Acts 17:1–8; compare 1 Thessalonians 2:1–14).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• Not that I am seeking a gift: Paul preferred to support himself financially (see Acts 18:3; 1 Corinthians 4:12; 1 Corinthians 9:3–18; 2 Corinthians 11:7–11; 2 Corinthians 12:14–15). 

• Paul was not seeking a gift for himself. Instead, he wanted their generosity to produce spiritual fruit, a reward from God credited to their account

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• Epaphroditus had carried the gifts from Philippi (see also Philippians 2:25–30).

• They are a fragrant offering: In the Old Testament, acceptable offerings were a pleasing fragrance to God (see Leviticus 1:9, Leviticus 1:13, Leviticus 1:17; Leviticus 2:2, Leviticus 2:9; Leviticus 3:5, Leviticus 3:16; compare Romans 12:1; Ephesians 5:2).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: After thinking about God's wonderful blessings, Paul ends the letter with words of praise to God.

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content: Some people in Caesar's household were believers working for the Roman government. Paul might have share the good news about Jesus with them while he was in prison. They might have been especially close to Paul and worried about him in prison (see Philippians 1:13).

entries.title: Philippians
entries.content:
• At the end of his letters, Paul often asks that the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with the people he is writing to (see also Philippians 1:2). Believers need Christ’s grace for both salvation and daily life. 

• Here, your spirit likely refers to the deepest part of the believers' inner being. The spirit is the part of the person that relates most directly to God. Paul is praying that Christ’s grace would strengthen and sustain them at the core of who they are.
